title: Vladimir Putin only has two options in Ukraine: Total victory or endless war
gist: Peter Dickinson argues US-led 'land for peace' efforts centered on ~6,000 sq km of Ukrainian-held Donetsk misread Putin, whose imperial goal is extinguishing Ukrainian statehood and whose regime now depends on wartime conditions. Absent decisive victory, Putin will likely prolong and escalate the war — already visible in intensified strikes on civilians, EU sabotage and record 2027 military spending — so peace requires much greater Western pressure.

insights.claim: US-led peace efforts are focused on an approximately 6,000 square kilometer stretch of Ukrainian-held land in Donetsk that Russia has been unable to seize militarily; US envoy Jared Kushner claims a deal is in place if Ukraine withdraws.
insights.so_what: The negotiating crux is narrow territorial; failure to resolve it keeps the war and associated risk premia in place.
insights.locator: US-led efforts to revive peace talks
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Zelenskyy told the UN that ceding the contested Donetsk land would embolden Putin to seek more cities such as Odesa, Kharkiv and Dnipro, and called the idea that Putin wants extra territory 'a crazy idea'.
insights.so_what: Kyiv's public rejection of territorial concessions lowers near-term ceasefire odds.
insights.quote: Putin doesn’t need extra kilometers, he needs Ukraine. He needs Ukraine to be part of Russia.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Critics say envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff treat negotiations as a geopolitical real estate deal, while the Kremlin views the war as a historic quest to extinguish Ukrainian statehood and revive the Russian Empire.
insights.so_what: Mismatch in frames implies deal-optimism from Washington should be discounted.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Putin sees reconquering Ukraine as the key to reversing the Soviet collapse, and further consolidation of Ukrainian statehood as a catalyst for Russia's further retreat from empire.
insights.so_what: Ideological rather than transactional motives make compromise settlements fragile.
insights.locator: To Putin, Ukraine is not only
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: A deal based on current front lines would limit Russian gains to roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, which Moscow would view as a major defeat, casting doubt on the durability of any such settlement.
insights.so_what: Even if a front-line deal is signed, renewed conflict risk would remain high.
insights.quote: Putin doomed to enter Russian history as the man who lost Ukraine
insights.locator: Crucially, Putin has framed his invasion
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Russian occupation authorities are erasing Ukrainian language, heritage and national identity in occupied areas.
insights.so_what: Reinforces the author's view that Russian aims are eliminationist, not territorial.
insights.locator: Long before the full-scale invasion began
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Putin has repeatedly refused an unconditional ceasefire and insists on addressing 'root causes', meaning sovereignty restrictions including a ban on NATO or other military alliances and significant limits on the size and capabilities of Ukraine's army.
insights.so_what: Kremlin demands amount to vassalization; ceasefire terms acceptable to Kyiv remain distant.
insights.locator: Almost everything about Putin’s present posture
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Putin said any deployment of European troops to Ukraine would mean 'war with Russia', which the author reads as intent to complete the conquest rather than a military concern, given European forces already sit in six NATO states bordering Russia.
insights.so_what: Undercuts European reassurance-force plans as a basis for a settlement.
insights.locator: Putin’s fierce opposition to a postwar European
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: The war has been woven into Russian statehood and bolstered Putinism, so a ceasefire would threaten the political, economic and social foundations of the regime.
insights.so_what: Russia's war economy is a regime-stability tool, making demobilization unlikely soon.
insights.quote: Despite its many costs, the war has bolstered Putinism and has been woven into the fabric of Russian statehood
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Putin likely wants to delay the return of more than half a million Russian soldiers, whose presence at home could destabilize Russia as Afghan war veterans did during the USSR's breakup.
insights.so_what: Demobilization risk is a hidden cost of peace for the Kremlin.
insights.locator: Putin is also no doubt eager
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: If Putin cannot secure decisive victory, he will almost certainly continue the war indefinitely rather than gamble on a compromise.
insights.so_what: Base case should be prolonged conflict, not a near-term peace dividend.
insights.quote: Putin will almost certainly opt to continue the war indefinitely rather than gamble on a compromise settlement
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: With Russian troops struggling to break through, Russia has dramatically increased round-the-clock bombardment of civilian targets across Ukrainian cities.
insights.so_what: Rising infrastructure damage raises Ukraine's energy import needs and reconstruction costs.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Russia is expanding sabotage and gray-zone aggression across the EU, and the Kremlin has unveiled plans for an enlarged army and record military spending in 2027.
insights.so_what: Supports sustained European defense spending and elevated security risk for EU infrastructure.
insights.locator: In parallel, Russia is expanding sabotage
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson

insights.claim: Serious negotiations will only begin when Putin is placed under considerably more pressure by Ukraine's allies — peace through strength.
insights.so_what: Implies further sanctions and military aid as the path to talks, not concessions.
insights.quote: Peace with Putin’s Russia is possible, but it can only be peace through strength.
insights.locator: The Russian ruler believes he is waging
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
